headline: Crashes involving Waymo robotaxis in Los Angeles County tripled last year as the fleet grew, though most were minor and Waymo says its crash rate per mile has fallen.
score_reason: Kept at the pool score: useful data on how driverless taxis perform as they spread, but the crashes are mostly minor and the paper itself says the data cannot yet settle who drives more safely.
importance_line: Riders, pedestrians and other drivers in cities where robotaxis are expanding are the people affected, and local officials such as San Diego's council are asking for more say, but the data cannot yet show whether driverless cars are safer overall and Waymo's own safety figures are company claims.
summary: The Los Angeles Times reports, from its review of crash data filed with the federal road-safety regulator NHTSA and a California crash dashboard, that crashes involving Waymo's driverless taxis in Los Angeles County rose from 69 in 2024 to 219 in 2025, with 186 so far this year, while just over 80% of this year's crashes caused no apparent injury and fewer than 1% a suspected serious injury. Waymo says its crash rate has fallen from about 57 to fewer than six per million miles and that its cars are safer than average drivers in the cities where it operates, but researchers quoted say the data cover only the conditions where robotaxis may run, skeptics say companies may under-report incidents, and one researcher says it cannot yet be said whether the industry at large is safer than human driving.
notes: Read in full. The LA Times' own analysis of official crash filings; its conclusion is contested, so REPORTED. The text holds inset related-story lines (for example about Zoox's Las Vegas launch and a Waymo car striking a child in Santa Monica) that are not part of the analysis and were not used. Robotaxis driving in Los Angeles is the machine action.
